title: Why Gratefulness Is a Predictor of Talent
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post distinguishes talent from skill, defining talent as how people learn and convert learning into improved performance. Among the many indicators of talent, the author highlights gratefulness as an overlooked signal. Grateful people reflect on experience more accurately and treat feedback as help rather than correction. The strongest reason, the author says, is relational: mentors and experts invest more in grateful people, who in turn credit others, share credit, behave fairly and accept responsibility for mistakes. This makes them desirable collaborators who are invited into learning opportunities and receive discretionary effort from others. Because talent grows through capable people and learning opportunities, which grateful team members attract, leaders are told to look at gratefulness when assessing talent.
points: Talent is defined as learning capacity rather than existing skill, which changes what leaders should look for.
Gratefulness is argued to improve reflection and the way feedback is received, as help instead of correction.
The main mechanism is relational, since mentors and experts invest more in people who show appreciation.
Grateful people share credit and own failures, making them preferred partners.
Leaders are advised to use gratefulness as a signal when separating talented people from merely skillful ones.
quotes: In contrast to skill, talent is about how people learn and turn that learning into a capacity to improve. Because of their ability to draw insights from experience and apply that learning to performance, talented team members excel more quickly than others, often with less formal training.

But the biggest reason gratefulness is such a strong sign of talent is relational. Experts and mentors are more likely to invest in a grateful person, so they receive more support from others and capitalize on the trust they are extended.

Grateful people are more likely to acknowledge the contribution of others early and often, share credit instead of hoarding it, behave fairly and with good intentions in social situations, and accept responsibility for failures or mistakes. This makes grateful team members more desirable as partners and colleagues.
Talent doesn’t grow in isolation. It needs other capable people and learning opportunities to develop. Grateful team members attract both.
For those who are genuinely talented, gratefulness magnifies their ability to learn, which is what talent is all about.
